questions.q: The resistance of a wire of length $l$ and cross-sectional area $A$ is:
questions.solution:
$R = \mathbf{\dfrac{\rho l}{A}}$.

Longer pipe, more resistance; wider pipe, less. Resistivity $\rho$ is the property of the material itself, independent of the shape you cut it into.

questions.q: The drift velocity of free electrons in a conductor is typically of the order of:
questions.solution:
Drift velocity is astonishingly slow — about $\mathbf{10^{-4}}$ m/s, a fraction of a millimetre per second.

The lamp still lights instantly because the **electric field** travels at nearly the speed of light and sets every electron in the wire moving at once.

A pipe already full of water: open the tap and water comes out immediately, though any one molecule crawls along.

questions.q: Two resistors of $6\,\Omega$ and $3\,\Omega$ are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac16 + \dfrac13 = \dfrac12 \Rightarrow R = \mathbf{2\,\Omega}$.

In parallel the answer is always less than the smallest branch — opening a second checkout lane can only shorten the queue.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule is a statement of the conservation of:
questions.solution:
The junction rule says the current in equals the current out — no charge piles up at a junction. That is **conservation of charge**.

The loop rule, by contrast, is conservation of **energy**: go round a closed loop and the potential returns to where it started.

questions.q: A cell of emf $\varepsilon$ and internal resistance $r$ drives a current $I$ through an external resistance $R$. The terminal voltage is:
questions.solution:
$V = \mathbf{\varepsilon - Ir}$ — some of the emf is spent driving the current through the cell's own resistance.

It is why a torch battery reads $1.5$ V unloaded and less while the bulb is on, and why an old battery 'sags' badly: $r$ has grown.

questions.q: A potential difference of $12$ V is applied across a $4\,\Omega$ resistor. Find the current, in amperes.
Find the power (in watts) dissipated in a $5\,\Omega$ resistor carrying a current of $2$ A.
questions.solution:
$P = I^{2}R = (2)^{2} \times 5 = \mathbf{20}$ W.

$P = VI$ and $P = V^{2}/R$ are the same law in different clothes — pick the form matching the quantities you were given.

questions.q: A wire of length $2$ m and cross-sectional area $1 \times 10^{-6}$ m$^{2}$ has resistance $4\,\Omega$. Find its resistivity in units of $10^{-6}\,\Omega$ m.
questions.solution:
$\rho = \dfrac{RA}{l} = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{2} = 2 \times 10^{-6}\,\Omega$ m.

So the answer is $\mathbf{2}$ (in units of $10^{-6}\,\Omega$ m).

questions.q: A cell of emf $2$ V and internal resistance $0.5\,\Omega$ is connected to a $1.5\,\Omega$ resistor. Find the current in amperes.
questions.solution:
$I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R + r} = \dfrac{2}{1.5 + 0.5} = \mathbf{1}$ A.

The internal resistance sits in series with everything else — forgetting it is the classic slip in this chapter.

questions.q: A current of $0.5$ A flows for $2$ minutes. Find the charge that passes, in coulombs.
questions.solution:
$q = It = 0.5 \times 120 = \mathbf{60}$ C.

Minutes must become seconds first — the ampere is a coulomb per **second**.

questions.q: Derive the relation $I = neAv_{d}$ between current and drift velocity.
questions.solution:
Let $n$ be the number of free electrons per unit volume, $A$ the cross-section, and $v_{d}$ the drift velocity.

In time $t$, every electron travels $v_{d}t$, so all the electrons in a cylinder of length $v_{d}t$ pass the chosen cross-section.

**Volume of that cylinder** $= A v_{d} t$.

**Number of electrons in it** $= n A v_{d} t$.

**Charge passing** $= neAv_{d}t$.

$I = \dfrac{q}{t} = \mathbf{neAv_{d}}$.

The whole derivation is one idea: count everybody who can reach the finishing line in time $t$.

questions.q: State the balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge and explain what 'balanced' means physically.
questions.solution:
With resistances $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ in the four arms and a galvanometer across the bridge, the balance condition is

$\mathbf{\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}}$.

**Physically**, balance means the two ends of the galvanometer sit at the **same potential**, so no current flows through it.

The bridge then reports a *ratio*, and the reading does not depend on the supply voltage or on the galvanometer's own resistance — which is why it measures an unknown resistance so precisely.

It is a null method: instead of measuring a quantity, you adjust until there is nothing to measure, and a zero can be spotted far more accurately than a number can be read.

questions.q: Two cells of emf $2$ V and $4$ V with internal resistances $1\,\Omega$ and $2\,\Omega$ are connected in parallel across an external resistance of $10\,\Omega$. Using Kirchhoff's rules, find the current through the external resistance.
questions.solution:
Let the potential across the parallel combination be $V$.

**Junction rule:** the currents the two cells deliver add up to the current through $R$.

Current from cell 1: $\dfrac{2 - V}{1}$. From cell 2: $\dfrac{4 - V}{2}$. Through $R$: $\dfrac{V}{10}$.

$\dfrac{2 - V}{1} + \dfrac{4 - V}{2} = \dfrac{V}{10}$.

Multiply by $10$: $20 - 10V + 20 - 5V = V \Rightarrow 40 = 16V \Rightarrow V = 2.5$ V.

$I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{2.5}{10} = \mathbf{0.25}$ A.

**Worth noticing:** $V = 2.5$ V is above cell 1's emf of $2$ V, so cell 1 is being **charged** by cell 2 — the current through it runs backwards. The algebra tells you that without your having to guess it in advance.

questions.q: Explain why the resistance of a metal increases with temperature while that of a semiconductor decreases.
questions.solution:
**Metals.** The number of free electrons hardly changes with temperature, but the lattice ions vibrate harder, so electrons collide more often and the relaxation time $\tau$ falls.

Since $\rho = \dfrac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}$, a smaller $\tau$ means a larger $\rho$ — **resistance rises**.

**Semiconductors.** Here heating breaks many more electrons free, so $n$ rises steeply — exponentially — and that swamps the fall in $\tau$.

$\rho$ therefore **falls**: a semiconductor conducts better when hot.

In a metal the crowd is fixed and the corridor gets busier; in a semiconductor the crowd itself multiplies.

questions.q: $n$ identical cells, each of emf $\varepsilon$ and internal resistance $r$, are connected in series across an external resistance $R$. Write the current, and say when this arrangement is better than connecting them in parallel.
questions.solution:
**In series:** the emfs add and so do the internal resistances.

$I = \dfrac{n\varepsilon}{R + nr}$.

**In parallel:** $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R + r/n}$.

**When series wins:** if $R \gg r$, the $nr$ hardly matters and the current is nearly $n$ times bigger. So series is for a **large external resistance**.

**When parallel wins:** if $R \ll r$, the internal resistance dominates, and dividing it by $n$ is what helps.

Rule of thumb: put the cells in series when the load is the bottleneck, in parallel when the cells themselves are.
